# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the strongest document in the set. It is randomised, uses record-based output, measures hours from system logs as well as timesheets, follows up for two years, and pre-registers the mechanism test. It directly answers the main open questions from the earlier documents, and both of its rebuttals are fair:

- **Against the re-analysis (Varga and Holm):** a gain survives when measured by the re-analysis's own standards.
- **Against the meta-analysis:** its decay evidence came from four uncontrolled studies that used scheduled hours, which is exactly the problem I flagged in that review.

The arithmetic checks out. The main issues are a misleading comparison in the Summary, contamination of the control arm that affects the decay estimate, an ambiguity in how log hours are defined that matters for the meetings mediation, and a confirmatory test run on the same offices that generated the hypothesis.

## 1. Arithmetic

**These check out:**
- Output per hour at 24 months: 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% on system logs.
- Halden survivors: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%), and 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%.
- Mediation shares: 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%.

**The Summary mixes two hours measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." But the 12.5% is a timesheet figure. The like-for-like decline is from 12.5% to 9.8%, about a fifth. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" falls between the two comparisons. The Summary should lead with 12.5% → 9.8% and report the 8.5% log figure separately as the stricter estimate.

**The decline itself is uncertain.** The 9-month interval (+6.9 to +18.4) and the 24-month interval (+4.6 to +15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is fair, but the change between time points should be tested directly, or the text should say it isn't statistically distinguishable from no change.

## 2. Control offices changed their meetings, which affects the decay estimate

The "unplanned observation" is contamination of the control arm, and it biases the 24-month estimate toward zero.

- Two of the seven control offices cut meetings in month 15 and raised output per hour by 4.1%. That lifts the control average by roughly 2/7 × 4.1 ≈ 1.2 points over the window the 24-month estimate covers.
- That is close to half of the 2.7-point decline on timesheets. Part of the apparent fading may be the control group improving, not the treatment effect shrinking.
- The audit came after the 9-month report publicised the meetings finding. That makes it plausibly a spillover of the trial's own results rather than a coincidence.

The report should:
- present the observation as contamination;
- report a sensitivity analysis excluding the two offices, or limited to months 1–14, with the caveat that excluding offices breaks randomisation;
- qualify its decay claim accordingly.

**A possible inconsistency in the meeting figures.** The overall control average moved only from 7.2 to 7.0 hours. If the two auditing offices fell to 5.0, the other five must have risen to about 7.8. That holds if offices are weighted equally; staff-weighting could change it. It is worth checking, because rising meeting time in most control offices would itself be notable.

## 3. How log hours are defined matters for the mediation result

Log hours are described as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases."

**If logs capture only casework, they exclude meetings.** Then the main way fewer meetings would raise output per hour, by moving time from meetings into casework, wouldn't appear in the outcome at all. The 47% meetings share would have to work through something else, such as less interrupted work. The interpretation changes completely.

**The figures suggest logs include more than casework:**

| | Control | Treated |
|---|---|---|
| Timesheet hours | about 37.9 | about 33.4 |
| Recurring meetings | 7.0 | 3.9 |
| Hours outside meetings | about 30.9 | about 29.5 |

On these figures, time outside meetings fell only about 4–5% relative to control, yet log hours fell 11%. That points to logs measuring logged-in session time, including meetings.

The report needs to define exactly what log time includes.

**A rough accounting calculation and the mediation estimate disagree.** On the figures above, output per hour outside meetings rose only about 1.4% (0.966 / 0.953). That implies meeting reductions account for around 85% of the 9.8% timesheet gain on a log scale, far above the mediation estimate of 47%.

The two methods can legitimately differ. Freed time need not all go to casework, and mediation estimates a causal pathway rather than an accounting identity. But the gap should be explained, since the simple accounting points to an even larger role for meetings.

## 4. The meetings test is pre-registered but not independent

Pre-registration at month 11, before the 24-month results, is a genuine improvement: it fixes the model and the outcome. But:

- **Same offices.** The hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices, and months 1–9 are inside the 24-month window. This is a pre-specified test on the same data, not a replication. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. Saying it answers the "post hoc" criticism goes too far.
- **Too few clusters.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information. With randomisation by office, the effective sample is still 7 v 7, and repeated months from the same office are not independent. A 95% CI of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. The report should state the method, such as an office-level bootstrap or a small-sample correction.
- **Correlated mediators.** Fewer meetings plausibly reduce fatigue. The report should say whether the mediators were estimated jointly, and how their overlap is handled.
- **Baseline meeting data.** The 9-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2) now appear, presumably extracted from calendars after the fact. That should be stated. It also resolves my earlier concern about missing baseline data.

## 5. The Halden follow-up

**A discretionary organisation reverted.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But the marketing agency cited client deadlines, and the meta-analysis would code marketing as discretionary work. It is a counterexample to the claim that discretionary work suits reduced hours, and should be reported as one rather than grouped with the coverage cases.

**Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations didn't provide data. Organisations that reverted or struggled are probably less likely to respond, so 3 reversions in 14 may understate the true rate.

**Baseline hours.** 40.3 is exactly the baseline for the 27 time-tracking organisations in Varga and Holm. Confirm that it is the baseline for these 11 organisations, and state how many of the 11 have time-tracking data. Only 17 of the original 23 had both records and time tracking.

**"Upper bound."** "Likely optimistic" is more accurate. Without a comparison group, general economic trends could push the estimate either way.

**Conflict of interest and attrition.** R. Okafor is an author of the original Halden paper. That should be disclosed in the Halden section. The report also doesn't address Varga and Holm's finding that seven withdrawals happened after the schedule began, contrary to the working paper. A follow-up co-authored by the Halden team is the natural place to correct that record.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Uncertainty.** Sick days (−27%), appeal overturn rates and resignations are again reported without intervals or difference-in-differences estimates.
- **Cost.** Overtime claimed in treated case-processing offices still isn't reported. Labour cost per case would complete the picture.
- **Counter-arm cost.** 12% more staff giving a 9% rise in cost per contact implies labour is about three-quarters of total cost. State the basis.
- **Decay estimate is likely conservative.** The account of the meta-analysis's duration subgroup is a strong point. Section 5 could add that Varden's own decline is likely overstated because of the control contamination.

## 7. What all five documents now support

> In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produces a cut of about 11–13% in actual hours and a gain in output per actual hour of about 8–10% that persists, somewhat reduced, at two years under randomised conditions. Output per employee is slightly below control, about 3%, with an interval that includes zero. Roughly half the per-hour gain operates through fewer recurring meetings, and perhaps more, though this rests on seven treated offices. Some of this may be achievable without cutting hours, a question no study has yet tested directly. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Claims that the model is sector-general, and claims that the gains are entirely an artifact, are both contradicted by the evidence.

The obvious next study is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, a meetings and process reorganisation at full hours, and a control group.

I can draft a referee report, a one-page synthesis of all five documents, or an outline of that three-arm trial design.
